title: Byzantine envoys at Piacenza
summary: Envoys of the Byzantine emperor Alexios I Komnenos reach a church council held by Pope Urban II at Piacenza. They ask for western knights to help fight the Turks, who since the Byzantine defeat at Manzikert in 1071 have taken most of Anatolia.
significance: Alexios wanted mercenaries under his own command. What he got eighteen months later was a mass movement he could not control.

title: Urban II preaches the crusade
summary: On a field outside Clermont, Pope Urban II calls on the knights of the West to stop fighting each other and go east, to help the Christians there and free Jerusalem. Those who go will have their sins forgiven. By later accounts the crowd shouts 'God wills it!'
significance: No text of the speech survives. The versions we have were written years later, after Jerusalem fell. But the idea of a penitential war spread fast, carried by preachers across France, Italy and Germany.

title: Massacre of the Jews of Mainz
stat: Hebrew chronicles: about 1,100 Jews killed at Mainz, after earlier attacks at Speyer and Worms
summary: Crusader bands under Count Emicho attack the Jewish communities of the Rhineland. At Speyer the bishop protects most of the Jews. At Worms and Mainz the bishops fail to, and hundreds are killed. Many choose to kill their families and themselves rather than accept forced baptism.
significance: Jewish chroniclers remembered 1096 as a catastrophe. Some crusaders asked why they should march thousands of miles to fight God's enemies while leaving those at home alone.

title: The People's Crusade destroyed
stat: Most of perhaps 20,000 pilgrims killed or enslaved
summary: Tens of thousands of poor pilgrims and minor knights, many following the preacher Peter the Hermit, reach Constantinople months before the main armies. Alexios ferries them across the Bosporus. Raiding towards Nicaea, they are ambushed by the army of the Seljuk sultan Kilij Arslan and slaughtered.
significance: Kilij Arslan concluded that crusaders were easy to beat. He would be wrong about the next army.

title: The princes at Constantinople
summary: Through the winter, armies led by Godfrey of Bouillon, Bohemond of Taranto, Raymond of Toulouse and others reach Constantinople. Alexios makes most of the leaders swear to hand back any former Byzantine lands they take. In return he gives supplies, guides and gold, and ferries them to Asia.
significance: The oaths caused lasting bitterness. The crusaders thought Alexios abandoned them at Antioch. The Byzantines thought the crusaders broke their word. Anna Komnene, the emperor's daughter, described the Franks as greedy and unstable.

title: Nicaea surrenders to the Byzantines
summary: The crusaders besiege Nicaea, the Seljuk capital, for seven weeks. Byzantine boats are hauled overland to the lake that guards its west wall. The garrison then surrenders in secret to Alexios's officers, and the crusaders wake to see Byzantine flags on the towers.
significance: The crusaders were denied the plunder they expected. Alexios treated the Turkish captives, including the sultan's family, well, which the Franks found suspicious.

title: Battle of Dorylaeum
summary: Kilij Arslan and the Danishmendid emir ambush the crusader vanguard under Bohemond. Turkish horse archers ride round the Frankish knights for hours, until the second half of the army arrives and catches them from the flank. The Turks flee and abandon their camp.
significance: It opened Anatolia to the crusade. One Frankish chronicler wrote that the Turks would be the best soldiers in the world if only they were Christian.

title: Baldwin takes Edessa
summary: Godfrey's brother Baldwin leaves the main army and rides east. The Armenian ruler of Edessa, Thoros, adopts him as son and heir. Within weeks a riot kills Thoros and Baldwin takes the city.
significance: The County of Edessa, mostly Armenian Christian, was the first crusader state. It was also the most exposed, reaching out across the Euphrates.

title: Antioch falls
summary: After eight months of siege and famine, an Armenian officer in the garrison named Firuz lets Bohemond's men in over the walls at night. The crusaders kill much of the Muslim population. The governor Yaghi-Siyan flees and is killed by Armenian peasants.
significance: Bohemond kept Antioch for himself, breaking the oath to Alexios. The Principality of Antioch lasted until 1268.

title: Defeat of Kerbogha
summary: Days after Antioch falls, a huge relief army under Kerbogha, the atabeg of Mosul, traps the crusaders inside the city. A pilgrim claims to have found the Holy Lance that pierced Christ. The starving crusaders march out, and Kerbogha's coalition, split by rivalries among its emirs, breaks and flees.
significance: Muslim writers blamed disunity more than Frankish strength. Kerbogha's allies distrusted him, and some left the field early.

title: Massacre at Ma'arra
stat: Numbers unknown. Ibn al-Athir's 100,000 is far more than the town held
summary: Raymond of Toulouse's troops storm the Syrian town of Ma'arrat al-Numan and kill or enslave its people. In the famine that follows, Frankish chroniclers themselves record that some crusaders ate the bodies of the dead.
significance: The horror was remembered in Arab tradition for centuries. Rank-and-file crusaders then forced their quarrelling leaders to march on to Jerusalem.

title: Fall of Jerusalem
stat: Ibn al-Athir: 70,000 killed. A Jewish letter of the time and modern estimates suggest about 3,000
summary: About 13,000 crusaders, out of perhaps 60,000 who left home, besiege the Fatimid-held city for five weeks. They build siege towers with timber from Genoese ships at Jaffa. On 15 July Godfrey's men cross from a tower onto the north wall. The crusaders kill most of the Muslims and Jews they find, including many who took refuge on the Temple Mount.
significance: Frankish chroniclers boasted of wading in blood. The Fatimid governor and his guard, who surrendered at the Tower of David, were allowed to leave. Surviving Jews were ransomed by communities in Egypt. Muslims and Jews were then barred from living in the city.

title: Battle of Ascalon
summary: The Fatimid vizier al-Afdal arrives too late to save Jerusalem. The crusaders surprise his army at dawn outside Ascalon and rout it. Most crusaders then go home.
significance: It secured the conquest, but Ascalon itself stayed Fatimid until 1153. Only a few hundred knights stayed to hold the new kingdom.

title: Baldwin I crowned King of Jerusalem
summary: Godfrey of Bouillon, who ruled Jerusalem as 'Advocate of the Holy Sepulchre', dies in July 1100. His brother Baldwin leaves Edessa to a cousin and is crowned the first Latin King of Jerusalem on Christmas Day at Bethlehem.
significance: Baldwin spent his reign taking the coastal cities with Italian fleets, paid with trading quarters. Most people in his kingdom remained Muslims and eastern Christians.

title: Tripoli falls
summary: Raymond of Toulouse began blockading Tripoli from a castle on a nearby hill in 1103 and died before it fell. Cut off by land and sea, the city surrenders to his son Bertrand and a Genoese fleet. The town is sacked.
significance: It created the fourth crusader state, the County of Tripoli. Later Arab writers said the city's great library, the Dar al-Ilm, was burned, though the story may be exaggerated.

title: The Field of Blood
stat: Walter the Chancellor: 700 knights and 3,000 foot soldiers killed
summary: Ilghazi, the Turkish ruler of Mardin and Aleppo, surrounds and destroys the army of Roger of Salerno, regent of Antioch. Roger is killed with almost all his men. The Franks call the place Ager Sanguinis, the Field of Blood.
significance: The worst Frankish defeat in a generation. Aleppo, which had suffered years of Frankish raids, celebrated. Ilghazi did not follow it up and Antioch survived.
wiki: Battle of the Field of Blood

title: The Knights Templar founded
summary: Hugh of Payns and a few French knights vow to live as monks and guard pilgrims on the roads. King Baldwin II gives them part of his palace in the al-Aqsa Mosque, which the Franks call the Temple of Solomon. The Hospitallers, who ran a hospital for pilgrims, also take up arms in the following decades.
significance: The military orders became the standing army of the Latin East, rich from gifts of land across Europe. They held the great castles and fought in every major battle until 1291.

title: Tyre surrenders
summary: A Venetian fleet and the army of the kingdom besiege Tyre, a port on a near-island, for five months. Its starving people surrender on terms and are allowed to leave with their goods.
significance: Venice got a third of the city. With Tyre taken, the Franks held the whole coast except Ascalon.

title: Zengi takes Edessa
summary: Imad ad-Din Zengi, atabeg of Mosul and Aleppo, besieges Edessa while its count, Joscelin II, is away. His engineers dig mines under the walls, which collapse after four weeks. The Franks in the city are killed or enslaved. The Armenian and Syrian Christians are spared.
significance: The first crusader state to fall. Muslim poets hailed Zengi as a champion of holy war, and the news led the Pope to call the Second Crusade.

title: Bernard of Clairvaux preaches at Vézelay
summary: The abbot Bernard of Clairvaux, the most famous churchman of his day, preaches the new crusade before King Louis VII of France. So many take the cross that cloth for crosses runs out. Later that year, in the Rhineland, Bernard stops a monk named Radulf from stirring up attacks on Jews.
significance: The Jewish chronicler Ephraim of Bonn credited Bernard with saving many lives. Conrad III of Germany also took the cross, so two kings led the crusade.

title: Crusaders take Lisbon
summary: A fleet of English, Flemish and German crusaders bound for the Holy Land stops in Portugal. They help King Afonso Henriques besiege Muslim Lisbon for four months. The garrison surrenders, but the crusaders sack the city anyway.
significance: The only lasting success of the Second Crusade. The Pope had also approved crusades in Spain and against the pagan Wends on the Baltic coast.

title: Conrad's army destroyed near Dorylaeum
summary: Conrad III's German army, short of food and water, turns back near Dorylaeum. Seljuk horse archers harass it until it breaks. Most of the foot soldiers are killed or captured. Louis VII's French army, on a coastal route, is mauled at Mount Cadmus in January.
significance: The Franks blamed the Byzantine emperor Manuel I for poor guides and supplies. Manuel, who had just made a truce with the Seljuks, was wary of two crusading armies at his gates.

title: Siege of Damascus fails
summary: Kings Louis, Conrad and Baldwin III attack Damascus, the one Muslim power that had been allied with Jerusalem against Zengi. After four days they move their camp to the east side, where there is no water or cover. With Nur ad-Din's army approaching, they retreat.
significance: A humiliation, and each side blamed treachery. Damascus, which had kept its distance from the Zengids, began to look to Nur ad-Din, who took it six years later.

title: Nur ad-Din takes Damascus
summary: Zengi's son Nur ad-Din, ruler of Aleppo, enters Damascus with the help of its people, who open the gates. For the first time since the crusaders arrived, Muslim Syria is united under one ruler.
significance: Nur ad-Din built madrasas and hospitals, and had a pulpit made for al-Aqsa, ready for the day Jerusalem was retaken. He made jihad the official cause of his state.

title: Manuel I enters Antioch
summary: The Byzantine emperor Manuel Komnenos rides into Antioch in a grand procession, with Prince Reynald of Châtillon walking at his stirrup and King Baldwin III riding behind. Reynald had raided Byzantine Cyprus, and had already begged forgiveness barefoot in the emperor's camp.
significance: For twenty years Byzantium was the protector of the crusader states. Manuel married a princess of Antioch and sent a fleet to help invade Egypt.

title: Saladin becomes vizier of Egypt
summary: Nur ad-Din and King Amalric of Jerusalem have fought for five years over Fatimid Egypt, rich but failing. Nur ad-Din's Kurdish general Shirkuh wins and becomes vizier to the Fatimid caliph. He dies two months later, and his nephew, Salah ad-Din Yusuf ibn Ayyub, takes his place.
significance: The Franks now faced enemies to the north, east and south. Saladin, aged about 31, was a Sunni officer serving a Shia caliph, and loyal, at least in name, to Nur ad-Din.

title: End of the Fatimid caliphate
summary: On Nur ad-Din's orders, Saladin has the Friday prayer said in the name of the Sunni Abbasid caliph of Baghdad instead of the Fatimid caliph. The last Fatimid caliph, al-Adid, young and ill, dies days later. Two centuries of Shia rule in Egypt end quietly.
significance: Saladin now held Egypt's wealth in his own right. Nur ad-Din began to suspect him of disloyalty, and the two were close to war when Nur ad-Din died.

title: Death of Nur ad-Din
summary: Nur ad-Din dies in Damascus, leaving an eleven-year-old son. In October Saladin rides in from Egypt and takes Damascus, saying he has come to protect the boy. Over twelve years he wins Aleppo and Mosul's submission, often by fighting other Muslim rulers.
significance: His critics called him a usurper. His admirers said he was gathering Islam's strength for holy war. By 1186 he ruled from Cairo to the Euphrates.

title: Battle of Myriokephalon
place: A mountain pass in Phrygia (site uncertain)
summary: Manuel I leads a large Byzantine army to take Konya, the Seljuk capital. Sultan Kilij Arslan II ambushes the long column in a mountain pass. Manuel escapes and makes peace, but his siege train and much of his army are lost.
significance: Manuel compared it to Manzikert. It ended Byzantine hopes of retaking central Anatolia and weakened the empire that had protected the crusader states.

title: Battle of Montgisard
summary: Saladin invades the kingdom and lets his army spread out to plunder. The sixteen-year-old King Baldwin IV, who has leprosy, leads a few hundred knights and Templars out of Ascalon and surprises it near Ramla. Saladin's army is routed and he barely escapes back to Egypt.
significance: Saladin's worst defeat. He learned caution and spent the next decade building his power before he risked everything on one battle.

title: Massacre of the Latins in Constantinople
summary: As Andronikos Komnenos marches on the capital to seize power, crowds turn on the city's Italian merchants, resented for their trade privileges. Thousands of Latins, mostly Genoese and Pisans, are killed or sold to the Turks. The Venetians had already been expelled in 1171.
significance: Western chroniclers remembered it as Greek treachery. It fed the hostility that ended in the sack of 1204.

title: Battle of Hattin
place: Horns of Hattin, above Lake Tiberias
stat: About 20,000 Franks against about 30,000 in Saladin's army. Almost the whole Frankish army killed or captured
summary: Saladin besieges Tiberias to draw out the Frankish army. King Guy of Lusignan marches it across dry hills in the July heat. Surrounded and without water, with smoke from burning grass blowing in their faces, the Franks are destroyed on a twin-peaked hill, the Horns of Hattin. The relic of the True Cross is captured.
significance: Saladin spared King Guy but beheaded Reynald of Châtillon with his own hand, and had about 200 captured Templars and Hospitallers killed. With no army left to defend them, almost all the kingdom's towns fell within months.

title: Saladin takes Jerusalem
stat: Perhaps 15,000 who could not pay the ransom were enslaved
summary: Balian of Ibelin defends the city with few knights and many refugees. After Saladin's miners breach the north wall, Balian threatens to destroy the holy places and kill the Muslim prisoners unless terms are given. Saladin agrees: the Franks may leave if they pay a ransom. Those who cannot pay are enslaved.
significance: Both sides noted the contrast with 1099. The cross was taken down from the Dome of the Rock and al-Aqsa was washed with rosewater. Eastern Christians could stay, and Saladin invited Jews back to settle. Only Tyre held out, saved by the newly arrived Conrad of Montferrat.

title: Siege of Acre begins
summary: Released by Saladin, King Guy marches a small army to Acre and besieges it. Saladin's army in turn surrounds the besiegers. For nearly two years, crusaders arriving by sea and Muslims holding the hills fight, starve and die of disease in a double siege.
significance: It became the central battle of the Third Crusade. Saladin's secretary, Baha ad-Din, recorded it in detail from the Muslim camp.

title: Massacre of the Jews of York
summary: As England prepares for Richard I's crusade, riots break out against Jews in several towns. In York the Jewish community takes refuge in the royal castle. Besieged by a mob led by local men who owed them money, most kill their families and themselves. The survivors are murdered when they come out.
significance: The rioters burned the records of their debts in the minster. It was the worst of the attacks on English Jews, who were expelled from England a century later, in 1290.

title: Frederick Barbarossa drowns
summary: The German emperor Frederick I, nearly seventy, leads the largest army of the Third Crusade overland. He fights his way through the Seljuk sultanate and takes Konya, then drowns in the Saleph river in Cilicia. Most of his army breaks up and goes home.
significance: Saladin's advisers had feared Frederick most. Muslim chroniclers saw his death as an act of God, and only a remnant of his army reached Acre.

title: Richard takes Cyprus
summary: On the way east, Richard I of England's fleet is scattered by storms and some ships are wrecked on Cyprus. Its Byzantine ruler, the self-proclaimed emperor Isaac Komnenos, mistreats the survivors. Richard lands, marries Berengaria of Navarre at Limassol, and conquers the island in a month.
significance: Cyprus went to the Templars and then to Guy of Lusignan. Ruled by his family for three centuries, it outlived the crusader states on the mainland.

title: Acre surrenders
summary: Philip II of France and Richard arrive with siege engines and fresh troops, and their catapults batter the walls. The starving garrison surrenders without Saladin's consent. It promises a ransom, the return of the True Cross and the release of Frankish prisoners.
significance: Acre became the capital of the kingdom for the next century. Philip went home within weeks, leaving Richard in command.

title: Execution of the Acre prisoners
summary: Talks over the surrender terms drag on and Saladin delays the first payment. Richard has the Muslim prisoners of the garrison led out in sight of Saladin's army and killed. Some accounts say women and children were among them.
significance: Richard wanted to march south without guarding thousands of captives. Muslim writers called it treachery, and Saladin killed Frankish prisoners in reprisal.

title: Battle of Arsuf
summary: Richard marches his army down the coast towards Jaffa, the fleet alongside, in a column so tight that Saladin's archers cannot break it. Near Arsuf, Saladin attacks in force. The Hospitallers charge before Richard's signal, and Richard throws in the rest of his knights to turn it into a victory.
significance: It restored Frankish morale and won back the coast, but Saladin's army was intact. Richard made Jaffa his base.

title: Treaty of Jaffa
summary: Twice Richard comes within a day's march of Jerusalem, and twice turns back, judging he could take it but not hold it. In August he saves Jaffa from Saladin with a few knights. Both sides are worn out. A three-year truce leaves the coast from Tyre to Jaffa to the Franks and Jerusalem to Saladin, with Christian pilgrims free to visit.
significance: Richard and Saladin never met, though Richard bargained for months with Saladin's brother al-Adil and once proposed that al-Adil marry his sister. The kingdom survived, now ruled from Acre.

title: Death of Saladin
summary: Saladin dies of fever in Damascus, aged about 55. He had given away so much that, his secretary wrote, there was not enough in his treasury to pay for his burial. His lands are divided among his sons and his brother al-Adil.
significance: Later Europe made him the model of a chivalrous enemy. Among Muslims he was honoured as the man who regained Jerusalem, though his heirs fought each other and, in 1229, handed the city back.

title: Riga founded: the Baltic crusades
summary: Bishop Albert founds Riga as a base to convert the pagan Livonians. In 1202 he creates a military order, the Sword Brothers, and popes grant crusade privileges to Germans who fight in the Baltic. Conquest and forced conversion follow, in Livonia and, from the 1230s, in Prussia under the Teutonic Knights.
significance: The Baltic crusades created German-ruled states in what are now Latvia, Estonia and Poland, which lasted long after 1291. For the local peoples they meant conquest, tribute and the loss of their old religion.

title: Crusaders sack Zara
summary: The Fourth Crusade has ordered a fleet from Venice for 33,500 men, but only about a third turn up and they cannot pay. The Venetian doge Enrico Dandolo offers a delay if they help him take Zara, a Christian city on the Adriatic that had rebelled against Venice. They take it despite the Pope's ban.
significance: Pope Innocent III excommunicated the crusaders, then lifted the ban on all but the Venetians. It set the pattern for a crusade steered by debt.

title: Sack of Constantinople
summary: The crusaders sail to Constantinople to put a Byzantine pretender, Alexios IV, on the throne in return for money and troops. When he is overthrown and murdered and the money dries up, they storm the city on 12 April. For three days they loot the greatest Christian city in the world, stripping churches, killing and raping.
significance: Baldwin of Flanders was crowned Latin emperor and Venice took a share of the empire. The Byzantine historian Niketas Choniates wrote that the Muslims had been kinder at Jerusalem. The split between the Latin and Greek churches hardened for good.

title: Massacre at Béziers
stat: Thousands killed. The legates' figure of 20,000 is probably too high
summary: Pope Innocent III calls a crusade against the Cathars, Christians the Church called heretics, in southern France. At Béziers, the first town the army reaches, the people refuse to hand over the Cathars among them. The crusaders break in and kill almost everyone, Catholic and Cathar alike, many in the churches.
significance: A monk later wrote that the papal legate said 'Kill them all, God will know his own'. The words are probably invented; the slaughter was real. The war handed the south to the French crown.

title: Francis of Assisi meets al-Kamil
summary: During a truce, the friar Francis of Assisi crosses the lines at Damietta to preach to Sultan al-Kamil. The sultan receives him courteously, listens, and sends him back unharmed. Francis fails to convert him.
significance: A rare peaceful meeting across the lines. Francis's friars later became the guardians of the Catholic holy places in Jerusalem, a role they still hold.

title: Damietta falls
summary: The Fifth Crusade attacks Egypt, the heart of Ayyubid power. After seventeen months of siege, crusaders enter Damietta and find most of its people dead of famine and disease. Sultan al-Kamil had offered to trade Jerusalem for Damietta, but the papal legate Pelagius refused.
significance: Holding Damietta, the crusaders hoped to conquer Egypt. The offer of Jerusalem was not made again until Frederick II's treaty ten years later.

title: The Fifth Crusade surrenders
summary: The crusaders march up the Nile towards Cairo in July, as the annual flood begins. Al-Kamil's forces open the dykes behind them and the army is trapped in the water. Pelagius gives up Damietta in return for the army's freedom.
significance: Al-Kamil's camp grew into the town of Mansurah, 'the victorious'. Frederick II, who had promised to come and did not, was blamed by the Pope.

title: Frederick II gets Jerusalem by treaty
summary: The Emperor Frederick II, excommunicated for delaying his crusade, arrives with a small army. He speaks Arabic and trades letters with al-Kamil, who wants a free hand against his nephew in Damascus. By the Treaty of Jaffa in February, al-Kamil hands over Jerusalem, Bethlehem and Nazareth for ten years. Frederick enters Jerusalem on 17 March and crowns himself in the Holy Sepulchre the next day.
significance: The Temple Mount stayed in Muslim hands, and the city had no walls, pulled down in 1219. Many Muslims were outraged at al-Kamil, and many Christians at a deal made by an excommunicate.

title: Fall of Montségur
summary: The mountain fortress of Montségur, the last major Cathar refuge, surrenders after a ten-month siege. About 200 Cathar believers who refuse to give up their faith are burned on a great pyre below the castle.
significance: It ended Cathar resistance in the south. The Inquisition, created to hunt heresy there, outlived the crusade.

title: Khwarazmians sack Jerusalem
summary: Khwarazmian horsemen, driven west by the Mongols and hired by the Ayyubid sultan of Egypt, as-Salih Ayyub, burst into Jerusalem. They kill many of the Christians, including those who try to leave, and loot the Holy Sepulchre.
significance: Christian rule in Jerusalem was over. The city would not have a Christian government again until 1917.

title: Battle of Forbie
summary: The Franks ally with the Ayyubid rulers of Damascus and Homs against Egypt. Near Gaza, the Egyptian army under the Mamluk commander Baybars, with the Khwarazmians, destroys them. The military orders lose almost all their knights.
significance: The last great army of the kingdom was gone. It was also the first great victory for Baybars, who would end the crusader states.

title: Louis IX takes Damietta
summary: King Louis IX of France, deeply pious, lands near Damietta with perhaps 15,000 men. The garrison panics and abandons the city, which falls without a fight.
significance: Louis waited months for the Nile flood to pass before marching on Cairo. The delay gave the Egyptians time to recover.

title: Battle of Mansurah
summary: The crusaders cross a branch of the Nile to attack the Egyptian camp. Louis's brother Robert of Artois charges ahead into the town of Mansurah, where Mamluk soldiers led by Baybars trap and kill him and most of the Templars with him. Louis holds his camp, but the army is stuck.
significance: Disease and hunger followed. On the retreat in April, Louis and his army were captured.

title: The Mamluks seize power
summary: The Ayyubid sultan's slave soldiers, the Mamluks, murder his son and heir Turanshah, who has tried to sideline them. Louis IX, a prisoner, pays a huge ransom and gives back Damietta. The Mamluk officers rule Egypt, at first through the late sultan's widow, Shajar al-Durr.
significance: The Mamluks were boys, mostly Turks from the steppe, bought as slaves and raised as soldiers. Their sultanate ruled Egypt and Syria until 1517. Louis spent four years in the Latin East rebuilding its defences.

title: Mongols sack Baghdad
stat: Tens of thousands to hundreds of thousands killed. Sources differ widely
summary: Hulagu, grandson of Genghis Khan, besieges Baghdad. The Abbasid caliph al-Mustasim surrenders, and the Mongols kill much of the population over a week and loot the city. The caliph is put to death.
significance: The Abbasid caliphate, five centuries old, ended. Some in the Latin East and Europe hoped the Mongols, many of whose commanders and wives were Christians, would be allies against Islam.

title: Battle of Ain Jalut
summary: The Mongols take Aleppo and Damascus early in 1260. When Hulagu withdraws most of his army after the Great Khan's death, the Mamluk sultan Qutuz marches north. The Franks of Acre let him pass through their land. At the spring of Goliath in Galilee, his army defeats the Mongol force left behind under Kitbuqa, who is killed.
significance: The first major defeat of a Mongol army in open battle. Weeks later Baybars murdered Qutuz and became sultan. Syria passed to the Mamluks.

title: Byzantines retake Constantinople
summary: Michael VIII Palaiologos, emperor in exile at Nicaea, sends a small force towards Constantinople. Finding the Latin fleet away, it slips in through a gate at night. The last Latin emperor, Baldwin II, flees.
significance: The Byzantine Empire was restored, but poorer and smaller. Frankish lords kept much of Greece, and the empire never fully recovered.

title: Nahmanides in Jerusalem
summary: Moses ben Nahman, a leading rabbi of Catalonia, reaches Jerusalem. He had been forced into exile after defending Judaism in a public debate before the king of Aragon. He finds the city half ruined after Mongol raids, with only two Jewish families, and sets up a synagogue in an abandoned house.
significance: His letter to his son describes the desolate city. Jews have prayed in the Old City almost continuously since.

title: Baybars takes Antioch
summary: Baybars has already taken Caesarea, Arsuf, Safed and Jaffa. He storms Antioch in four days. Most of its people are killed or enslaved, and the city never recovers. Baybars writes to its absent prince, Bohemond VI, describing the slaughter in detail.
significance: The second crusader state ended after 170 years. Chroniclers on both sides reported huge numbers killed or captured.

title: Louis IX dies at Tunis
summary: Louis IX sets out on a second crusade, but lands at Tunis, perhaps hoping to convert its ruler or win a base. Disease sweeps the camp in the summer heat. Louis dies of dysentery on 25 August.
significance: He was made a saint in 1297. His was the last great royal crusade. The English prince Edward went on to Acre in 1271 but could do little.

title: Krak des Chevaliers surrenders
summary: Baybars besieges the Hospitallers' great castle, held by a small garrison. After his miners take the outer wall, the knights hold out in the inner castle, then surrender after a forged letter tells them to.
significance: The strongest crusader castle fell in little over a month. It shows how thinly the orders were spread by then.

title: Tripoli falls
summary: Sultan Qalawun besieges Tripoli, a rich trading city split by quarrels among its Frankish lords and the Genoese and Venetians. After a month of bombardment his troops storm it. Men are killed, women and children enslaved, and the city razed.
significance: Qalawun built a new Tripoli a few miles inland. Only Acre and a few coastal towns were left to the Franks.

title: Fall of Acre
summary: Sultan al-Ashraf Khalil besieges Acre with a huge army and about a hundred siege engines. After six weeks his troops break through at the Accursed Tower. Those who can flee to ships. Thousands are killed or enslaved. The Templars' fortress by the sea holds out until 28 May.
significance: Tyre, Sidon, Beirut and the last castles were abandoned within weeks. Two centuries of crusader rule on the mainland were over, though crusades were preached and fought for centuries more.
